passage:
My name is Jagdish, and I still remember the envelope. It was addressed to my wife, Afreen, but it had the bank's name in the window, so I opened it thinking it was about our joint account. It wasn't. It was a reminder for a loan of four lakh rupees, in her name, taken eight months earlier. I read it three times standing by the shoe rack.
When she came home, I just held it up. She went pale and said, "It was for Imran's shop. I was going to tell you."
Eight months. I had sat beside her at her brother's shop opening and clapped. I felt like the only person in the room who hadn't been told the joke.
That night I lay awake going through everything: the phone she said was a gift, the late evenings, the savings figure she always rounded off. What else?

qa.q: What did Afreen say the loan was for?
qa.a: Afreen said it was for Imran's shop.

qa.q: What does Jagdish's sleepless night suggest he is thinking?
qa.a: Jagdish has started doubting everything, going back over the phone, the late evenings and the savings figure and wondering what else Afreen has hidden.

qa.q: At this first stage, what could help Jagdish before the next talk with Afreen?
qa.a: Jagdish could take a little time for the shock to settle, then ask Afreen for the whole story calmly instead of piecing it together alone at night. Talking to a trusted friend or a counsellor could also help.

qa.q: What might Afreen be going through when Jagdish holds up the letter?
qa.a: Afreen is likely frightened and ashamed, caught between protecting her brother and facing her husband. Going pale and saying 'I was going to tell you' suggests she knew this moment would come.

grounding: Shows a husband discovering his wife's hidden loan for her brother, with shock, a sense of being made a fool, and sudden doubt about other secrets.

passage:
Note for file, Tuesday. Siddharth, shift supervisor.
Around eleven, Manoj took a call at his desk and went very still. He asked the caller to repeat the amount twice and wrote nothing down. Then he stepped into the corridor and phoned his wife. I heard, "For Rakesh? Your brother's shop? Eight months and you said nothing?"
When he came back he stared at his screen without typing for almost twenty minutes. Then he asked me, quite seriously, whether there was any way to check if other loans had his address on them. He laughed once, not a happy laugh: "Last to know in my own house."
His hand shook when he picked up his water bottle.
I did not ask for details. I told him to take the afternoon off, reminded him the staff counselling line is free and private, and said the report could wait. He left at one. I will check in with him quietly tomorrow.

qa.q: How long did Manoj stare at his screen without typing?
qa.a: Manoj stared at his screen without typing for almost twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Manoj's question about other loans suggest he is worried about?
qa.a: It suggests Manoj suddenly fears there may be more hidden debts; one secret has made him doubt what else he does not know.

qa.q: How did Siddharth support Manoj at this stage, and what else could help?
qa.a: Siddharth gave Manoj the afternoon off, mentioned the free, private counselling line and did not pry. Once the first shock passes, a calm talk with his wife, perhaps with a counsellor, could be a next step.

qa.q: How might Manoj's wife be feeling after his call?
qa.a: She is probably scared and ashamed now that the secret is out, and may be bracing for his anger while still worried about her brother Rakesh.

grounding: Illustrates the moment a husband learns of a large loan his wife took for her brother, and his shock, humiliation and doubt, as seen by his supervisor.

passage:
The letter from the bank in Malmö was addressed to Ulla, but Henrik opened it by mistake while sorting the post at the kitchen counter. A repayment reminder. A loan he had never heard of, taken out eleven months ago, for more than they had saved in five years.

He read it twice. Then he looked around the flat as if it belonged to someone else: the new kettle, the calendar with her brother Jonas's birthday circled in red.

When Ulla came in with the shopping, he held up the page. "Is this real?"

She set the bags down very slowly. "Jonas's workshop was going under. I was going to tell you."

Henrik laughed once, without any humour. He thought of every evening he had sat with her going over their budget, nodding. What else had she been nodding through?

qa.q: What did Henrik open by mistake while sorting the post?
qa.a: He opened a letter from the bank addressed to Ulla, a repayment reminder for a loan he had never heard of.

qa.q: How can you tell Henrik feels made a fool of, not just surprised?
qa.a: He laughs once without humour and remembers all the evenings he sat going over their budget with her, nodding; he feels humiliated and shocked, and suddenly doubtful about what else she hid.

qa.q: What small step could help Henrik in the next hour, before the conversation turns into a fight?
qa.a: He could say plainly that he is too shocked to talk well right now and agree a time later that day to hear the whole story, instead of cross-examining her in the doorway.

qa.q: What might Ulla be feeling as she sets the bags down so slowly?
qa.a: She is probably frightened and ashamed, caught before she was ready, and torn between loyalty to Jonas and knowing she has hurt Henrik.

grounding: Henrik learns that his wife Ulla hid a large loan taken for her brother and is left shocked, humiliated and doubting what else he has missed.

passage:
The loan officer at the bank branch in Aizawl turned her screen so Farhan could see it. "Sir, before we process the home loan, there is an existing personal loan in your wife's name. The repayments come from your joint account."

Farhan stared at the number. Lalremsiami sat beside him, filling in the address section, and her pen stopped.

"There must be a mistake," he said, and heard how thin his voice was.

He turned to her. "What is this?"

She did not look up. "It was for my brother Mapuia's college fees. Last year. I meant to—"

The officer found a sudden interest in her stapler. Farhan felt heat climb up his neck. Two strangers in the queue behind them had heard. He had been the one explaining to the officer how careful they both were with money. Now he sat there wondering which other papers in their cupboard he had never read.

qa.q: Where do Farhan and Lalremsiami find out about the loan?
qa.a: At the bank branch in Aizawl, when the loan officer checks before processing their home loan.

qa.q: What is Farhan feeling when heat climbs up his neck?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and shocked, because he had just told the officer how careful they both were, and strangers in the queue heard.

qa.q: What could Farhan do right there at the desk to avoid making things worse?
qa.a: He could ask the officer to pause the application and say to Lalremsiami that they will talk about it at home today, so the first real talk is not in front of strangers.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami experience this moment?
qa.a: She is likely mortified that it came out in public and afraid of Farhan's reaction, while still believing she helped Mapuia for a good reason.

grounding: The passage shows a husband's shock and sense of being made a fool when a bank officer reveals his wife's hidden loan for her brother's college fees, and his sudden doubt about other papers.

passage:
Jahnavi,

I am writing this at two in the morning on the balcony because if I try to say it out loud I will shout, and I don't want Pinky to wake up to that.

I saw the SMS from the lender on your phone when you asked me to check the train timing. Four lakh. Taken in March. For Mahesh bhaiya's shop, I suppose, since he suddenly had new shutters in April.

I keep thinking of the Diwali dinner at your mother's, when Mahesh thanked "both of us" and I smiled like an idiot because I didn't know what he meant. Everyone at that table knew except me.

And now I'm lying awake going through every "it's nothing, just office" you said this year. I don't know which ones were true.

I'm not leaving. I just need you to tell me everything, all at once, tomorrow.

Your husband,
Jagdish

qa.q: When and where is Jagdish writing the letter?
qa.a: At two in the morning on the balcony.

qa.q: Why does the Diwali dinner memory hurt Jagdish so much?
qa.a: He realises everyone at that table knew about the loan except him, so he feels humiliated and betrayed, like he was the only fool in the room.

qa.q: Was writing a letter instead of talking straight away a good choice, and why?
qa.a: It was a sensible choice: he avoids shouting while Pinky sleeps, and he says clearly what he needs next, which is a full account tomorrow.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi feel when she reads that he is going through every "it's nothing, just office"?
qa.a: She may feel ashamed and scared, seeing that one hidden loan now makes all her small everyday words look doubtful to him.

grounding: Jagdish's letter shows a husband's shock, humiliation and new doubt about everything else after finding the loan his wife took for her brother.

passage:
People keep asking me why I've gone quiet at work. So here it is. I'm Tejas, Mehr's husband of two years, and last Tuesday a bank letter came to the flat addressed to her.

I opened it by mistake. It was a repayment notice. For a loan I'd never heard of. A big one.

When she came home, she went white. She said it was for her brother Asif, for his shop, eight months ago. She'd been paying it quietly every month.

I remember standing in the kitchen feeling like the whole building had tipped. And then this hot, burning feeling: I'm the fool here. Everyone knew but me? Did Asif know I didn't know?

The worst part came that night. Lying awake, I started going through everything. The new phone she said was a gift. The weekend at her mother's. What else?

qa.q: Who was the loan for?
qa.a: The loan was for Mehr's brother Asif, for his shop.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling in the kitchen?
qa.a: He felt shocked and humiliated, a burning sense of being made a fool, followed by doubt about what else was hidden.

qa.q: What could help Tejas at this raw stage?
qa.a: He could avoid big decisions for a few days and tell Mehr he needs the whole story, calmly, rather than questioning every past memory alone at night.

qa.q: How might Mehr have felt when she saw the letter was opened?
qa.a: Mehr likely felt panic and shame, knowing the secret she had kept for eight months was out.

grounding: A husband discovers his wife hid a large loan for her brother and feels shock, humiliation and a sudden doubt about everything else.
